summary: Cambodia lies in the south of the Indochinese Peninsula, the birthplace of the ancient Khmer Empire. It is famous for Angkor Wat and in modern times suffered the tragedy of Khmer Rouge rule.

ranking.name: Theravada Buddhism
ranking.description: From the 13th century, Theravada Buddhism, introduced via Sri Lanka and Siam, replaced Hinduism and Mahayana Buddhism in the late Angkor period and became the faith of the common people; after the 14th century kings also converted, and Buddhism became closely bound up with Khmer kingship and village life. Buddhism was destroyed under the Khmer Rouge (1975–1979), with monks mostly killed or forced to disrobe, but it revived rapidly after 1979, was made the state religion by the 1993 constitution, and temporary ordination of men remains a common custom.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Cambodia's Muslims are mainly the Cham, descendants of the ancient kingdom of Champa; after Vietnam's southward expansion destroyed Champa between the 15th and 19th centuries, large numbers moved into Cambodia, and converted to Islam around that time. The Cham suffered particularly severe persecution under the Khmer Rouge, and today live mainly in Kampong Cham Province and in fishing villages along the Mekong River.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Portuguese and Spanish missionaries first came to Cambodia in the 16th century, and Catholic missionary activity expanded during the French colonial period of 1863–1953, but the believers were mostly of Vietnamese descent. The Catholic cathedral in Phnom Penh was demolished under the Khmer Rouge. After the 1990s, evangelical Protestant groups entered in large numbers, preaching in villages and among the urban poor, and the number of believers has grown.

religion.background: Cambodia was influenced early by Indian culture, and the kings of Funan and the Angkor dynasty (9th–15th centuries) worshiped Hinduism and Mahayana Buddhism; Angkor Wat, built in the 12th century, was originally a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu. From the 13th century Theravada Buddhism, introduced via Sri Lanka and Thailand, spread among commoners, and after the 14th century became the mainstream, continuing to this day. In 1975–1979 the Khmer Rouge regime abolished all religion, killed large numbers of monks and demolished temples, nearly wiping out Buddhism. In 1989 Buddhism was again made the state religion, and the 1993 constitution confirmed its status; today temples and monks are once again at the center of village life.

ranking.name: Khmer
ranking.description: The Khmer are Cambodia's main ethnic group, and the Khmer language has been the language of the Angkor dynasty since ancient times, with inscriptions from the 7th century onward continuing to the present. After independence in 1953, Khmer became the national language and the sole official language, used in all schools, government and media, so almost the entire population has it as a mother tongue or common language.

ranking.name: Vietnamese
ranking.description: The history of Vietnamese in Cambodia goes back to the 17th century, when Vietnam expanded into the Mekong Delta, and during the French colonial period large numbers of Vietnamese were recruited as civil servants and laborers. The Lon Nol regime in 1970 and the Khmer Rouge regime in 1975 expelled and massacred Vietnamese; after Vietnam sent troops to overthrow the Khmer Rouge in 1979, some Vietnamese returned to Cambodia, living mainly in the floating villages of Tonle Sap and in Phnom Penh.

language.history: Khmer belongs to the Mon-Khmer branch of the Austroasiatic family and is one of the oldest written languages in Southeast Asia, with the earliest surviving Khmer inscriptions dating to the 7th century. The Khmer of the Angkor era absorbed large amounts of Sanskrit and Pali vocabulary, and the Khmer script derives from the Pallava script of southern India and later influenced the Thai and Lao scripts. During the French colonial period of 1863–1953 French became the language of administration and the elite; after independence in 1953 Khmer became the sole official language, and from the 1970s it gradually replaced French in education.

ranking.name: Fish amok
ranking.localName: អាម៉ុកត្រី (Amok trey)
ranking.description: Fish is mixed with a spice paste (kroeung) pounded from lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and kaffir lime leaves and with coconut milk, placed in a banana-leaf bowl and steamed, giving a mousse-like texture.
ranking.history: Amok is regarded as Cambodia's national dish and makes use of the abundant freshwater fish of Tonle Sap and the Mekong. Some think it originated in Khmer court cuisine, but there is no early documentary proof; Thailand and Laos also have similar steamed fish curries. Under the Khmer Rouge many traditional dishes disappeared along with their cooks, and after the 1990s amok became Cambodia's representative dish again as tourism developed.

ranking.name: Num banh chok (Khmer noodles)
ranking.localName: នំបញ្ចុក (Num banh chok)
ranking.description: Fine rice noodles pressed from fermented rice batter, topped with a yellow-green curry broth cooked with fish, lemongrass and turmeric, served with plenty of raw vegetables and herbs.
ranking.history: Num banh chok is often called "Khmer noodles" and is Cambodia's most common breakfast, sold by vendors carrying shoulder poles along the streets. Making the noodles requires soaking and fermenting the rice and then pressing it, traditionally done collectively by the women of the village. At weddings and religious festivals, families also prepare the noodles as offerings to monks and to entertain guests; similar rice foods are said to be mentioned in Angkor-era inscriptions, but details are unclear.

ranking.name: Kuy teav (noodle soup)
ranking.description: A clear, pork-bone broth with flat rice noodles, pork, shrimp and offal, served with bean sprouts, lime and herbs. The broth is clear and sweet, and chili and lime are added to individual taste when eating.
ranking.history: Kuy teav originates in the noodle soup brought by Teochew Chinese immigrants, and the word "kuy teav" is in fact the Teochew pronunciation of "guotiao". From the 19th to the early 20th century large numbers of Teochew people moved to Cambodia to trade and opened noodle stalls in cities such as Phnom Penh, and the dish gradually became localized and one of Cambodia's most common breakfasts. In southern Vietnam it is also popular under the name "hủ tiếu Nam Vang" (Phnom Penh noodles).

ranking.name: Lok lak (beef stir-fry)
ranking.description: Chunks of beef marinated in soy sauce, oyster sauce and sugar are quickly stir-fried, served with lettuce, tomato, white rice and a lime-and-black-pepper dipping sauce. The beef is tender and juicy, and the dip is tangy, spicy and peppery.
ranking.history: Lok lak is generally thought to have arisen during the French colonial period (1863–1953) under Vietnamese and French culinary influence; Vietnam has a similar "shaking beef" (bò lúc lắc), and both names imitate the sound of the wok being shaken. The Cambodian version is notably served with black pepper from Kampot and a lime juice dip, and sometimes topped with a fried egg.

ranking.name: Prahok (fermented fish paste)
ranking.description: Small fish are headed, scaled, pounded and salted, then fermented in earthen jars for weeks to years to make a pungent fish paste, which can be eaten raw, steamed, or stir-fried into dishes as seasoning.
ranking.history: Prahok is the Khmer people's ancient way of preserving protein: each dry season when the water level of Tonle Sap falls, large catches of fish are taken, and people salt and ferment them to eat in seasons when the catch is small. It is called "Cambodia's cheese", and during the Khmer Rouge period and the famine years of the civil war prahok was the food many families relied on to survive. To this day, during the fishing season from December to February, whole families can still be seen making prahok by Tonle Sap.
